HEADLINE: The 'war room' that helped to seal cricket deal
TEXT:
Inside the deal Hosting the Comm Games was fortuitous for Seven.

Locked in what Seven West Media had nicknamed "the war room" in the luxury The Star hotel and casino resort on the Gold Coast, billionaire proprietor Kerry Stokes, his son Ryan and Tim Worner worked late into the night last Thursday to save the free-to-air broadcaster's summer schedule and in the process change the entire network.

Having recently lost Australian Open and other tennis rights from 2020 onwards, Seven executives, on the Gold Coast for the Commonwealth Games, were determined to make sure they secured the deal as the new home of cricket on free-to-air television.

Without that strategy, and the serendipitous timing of having all the network's executives in the one place for the Games, Seven executives admit they would never have won the cricket rights as part of a near $1.2 billion deal Cricket Australia pulled off last week with Foxtel and its News Corporation bosses, that left rival networks feeling upset, confused and betrayed.

The deal leaves Seven with the AFL and cricket for the first time, Foxtel being able to boast having a big summer sport ahead of its planned IPO, Nine Entertainment having lost cricket after 40 years but gained tennis, and Network Ten with virtually no sport.

It also means cricket has more money than ever and some rare good news after the recent ball tampering controversy.

It was a stunning week.

While Sydney was the epicentre of the cricket deal, up on the Gold Coast Seven's war room ranged to as many as 12 people, including programming, legal, finance, sales and production executives, to as few as three. Commercial director Bruce McWilliam also worked over the deal on the Gold Coast and back in Sydney.

But in the last hours before final free-to-air bids were due at 11.45pm on Thursday, it was just Stokes and Worner, having tense conversations with Cricket Australia boss James Sutherland. Talks also took place with News Corp and Foxtel executives, including Siobhan McKenna, Patrick Delany, Michael Miller and Peter Campbell, who had sealed the pay TV component deal, as revealed by The Australian Financial Review, which would see the sport announce a record $1.18 billion six-year deal.

"I don't think we could have got there if we hadn't been there in the same place. The Comm Games was fortuitous timing for us," Worner told the Financial Review.

"But we were trying to make sure the euphoria of the ratings high we were getting at the Comm Games didn't effect us in the cricket talks. We needed to be cool about as much as we could."

Ten, which had held the Big Bash League under the previous TV deal and grown the sport from a $20 million property no free-to-air broadcaster wanted into the crown jewel of Cricket Australia's rights, submitted its final bid late on Thursday to be Foxtel's partner after a frustrating day with the sporting body for the CBS-owned network.

Earlier in the week, Ten had submitted a new bid which would see the CBS-owned network take all of Cricket Australia's broadcast rights for around $960 million over six years. Cricket Australia refused the offer. CA had been negotiating with Foxtel on Wednesday and locked in the major parts of the deal in late night negotiations believed to have been at New Corp's Holt Street headquarters in Sydney.

The sporting body also kept negotiating with Seven on Wednesday night and Thursday morning and when Ten reached out again were told by Cricket Australia to engage with Foxtel.

Sources said it became clear to Ten that all that was left for free-to-air was to simulcast Test matches and 43 BBL games and Foxtel had sealed its deal for every ball of cricket played in Australia. Ten was told by Cricket Australia a number it needed to get to and with CBS' blessing put an offer in for $80 million a year, $70 million cash, $10 million contra, or $480 million over six years, to partner with Foxtel.

At close to 5.15pm on Thursday, Ten and Cricket Australia shook hands on a deal to make Ten the free-to-air partner for cricket, and Ten chief executive Paul Anderson signed a binding bid with a heads of agreement to be signed once drafted.

Cricket Australia denies a handshake deal and the binding bid was just that - a bid - and hadn't committed to Ten.

However, Ten's team, which included Anderson, David Barham and Stuart Thomas, left Credit Suisse offices in Sydney, where Cricket Australia had based itself, with the expectation its bid wasn't going to be shopped to rivals, BBL return to their network and Test matches come to Ten for the first time under a simulcast arrangement with Foxtel, and they would be returning to negotiate a heads of agreement later that night.

"We have no problems with how the process unfolded and how we went about it. It was a fair process and we have no regrets about it," Sutherland said. Cricket Australia is adamant it played the process fairly.

Around 8pm, Sutherland called Anderson and Worner telling them they needed submit best and final bids. CBS executives were asleep in the US, and the bid deadline was pushed back until 11.45pm.

In the end, Ten put in a $80 million per season bid and pushed that they hoped their relationship with Cricket Australia would continue, given what it had done for the BBL franchise over the last five years. Seven bid $82 million per season, $75 million in cash and $7 million contra.

Crucially, Seven's bid was slightly higher in cash terms. It was a small but important point for a sporting body that has recently lost sponsors such as Magellan Financial Group in the wake of the ball tampering scandal.

Sutherland contacted both Worner and Anderson separately at 2am on Friday the 13th informing them of the outcome, which was revealed by the Financial Review only hours later. Seven won, Ten lost.

The process had ended with a result which nobody could have predicted where both incumbent broadcasters would no longer partner with Cricket Australia, and in particular one that led to cricket's 40-year relationship with Nine ending. In late February, Nine chief executive Hugh Marks reached out to Anderson about a potential tie-up on cricket. Marks had been working with Fox Sports, but hadn't come to an agreement yet.

Nine had its eye on Tennis Australia's upcoming rights and a partnership with Ten, which would see Test matches stay on Wide World of Sports and CBS' newly purchased Australian network retain BBL and take on international limited overs cricket for the first time, and believed it made financial sense.

Nine and Ten were also open to working with Fox Sports. Nine had previously negotiated with Fox Sports about a potential joint-bid, because bringing in pay TV in some capacity would help get to the lofty outcome Cricket Australia wanted.

When Cricket Australia put out their tender in mid-March, the sporting body gave less than two weeks for interested parties to work out their bids. Nine, Ten and Fox Sports couldn't come to an agreement in the time frame, Nine and Ten only reached their agreement on April 16, and the pay TV provider submitted its own bid for the whole package, while the pair of free-to-air networks submitted a joint $130 million per season bid. Seven also submitted a bid, noting it would need a partner.

Nine and Ten's joint-bid did not break down what they would pay each for Cricket Australia's 11 different broadcast packages. Marks and Anderson flew to Melbourne the afternoon bids were due on March 19 for a meeting with Cricket Australia at 5pm.

Sutherland was in Dubai, but Marks and Anderson met Cricket Australia's media rights team Ben Amarfio and Stephanie Beltrame as well an in-house lawyer and an external lawyer.

The pair of television executives were keen to explain why they had bid together. The meeting was over in 15 minutes. By the end of the week, Cricket Australia had rejected the joint-bid as non-compliant in a short two-line email to the general counsels of both Nine and Ten. Cricket Australia chairman David Peever had even slammed Ten's local management as "bottom feeders."

On March 28, Cricket Australia told Nine and Ten they would not engage until the JV was dissolved. On March 29, Nine announced its swoop on Tennis Australia's broadcast rights.

Once Nine secured tennis, it handed negotiating of cricket to Anderson. Marks was still keen to hold onto Test matches, but was adamant and upfront with Ten that Nine would not be overspending on cricket.

On Thursday April 5, Ten resubmitted an all free-to-air bid worth $900 million over six years, where it would sub-licence Test matches to Nine, for the same price as the network had paid under the previous deal. Cricket Australia did not engage until the following Monday when Sutherland, Amarfio and Beltrame flew to Sydney.

On the morning of Friday April 6, Cricket Australia and Foxtel had nearly nailed down their deal. Campbell was negotiating via phone conference, and 12 of 14 legal points in the contract been drawn up had been worked through.

Campbell ended the call out of frustration. The Fox Sports chief operating officer was annoyed having been led to believe they were close to a deal, Cricket Australia came back to them with more issues and it was clear they were still talking with Ten.

Miller texted Peever that afternoon that Fox Sports was still keen on cricket.

News Corp's The Australian decried Cricket Australia, claiming the body's "rights hope hit for six as Foxtel, Fox Sports bail". Less than a week later, Foxtel had sealed a deal with Cricket Australia and is now partnered with Seven. While the outcome was known the morning of last Friday, the details were not finalised between all the parties.

Cricket Australia set a 2pm press conference on Friday, but Miller and Delany were still up in Credit Suisse's office negotiating on the phone with Worner and Stokes, who were already at the Intercontinental Hotel, through the final points of the contract.

Miller came down to the in Sydney around 2.30pm, while Delany walked the two blocks near Circular Quay around 3pm. The duo enjoyed a beer soon after the announcement was made official.

Worner, meanwhile, flew back to the Gold Coast and joined the Stokes father and son duo at Seven's corporate entertainment precinct at the Commonwealth Games that. After a quick trip to Rebel Sports, Seven staff had decked out the area with cricket bats, balls and stumps adorned with Seven stickers.

It was a celebration of a pivotal moment in Australian broadcasting and sport, one which sees the biggest amount of sports content move networks ever.

I don't think we could have got there if we hadn't been there in the same place. The Comm Games was fortuitous timing for us. Tim Worner, Seven West Media CEO

HEADLINE: MasterChef recipe still cooking for Network Ten a decade on
TEXT:
When MasterChef was presented to advertisers and clients at Network Ten's 2008 upfronts, the reaction, to put it politely, was muted.

Ten had squeezed all it could out of reality show Big Brother and it was looking for a new show to fill the void. But, a reality cooking competition program had plenty of doubters.

Ten chief content officer Beverley McGarvey, who was part of the team which dreamed up the Australian version of MasterChef nearly a decade ago, admits the show had a "very poor reception" and there were questions about cooking as a reality genre.

"The show was pitched for Ten by Mark and Carl Fennessy who were at Fremantle at the time. It was the result of a real requirement from us, we had decided to move on from Big Brother," Ms McGarvey told The Australian Financial Review.

"It was seen at the time as quite a bold move to take a one hour a week British cooking show, which had a tone to it, and super size it."

Ten took a chance and built MasterChef as a six-night a week franchise in its first season.

"It was an instant hit and then it grew. It was a moment-in-time thing," Ms McGarvey said.

Endemol Shine chief executive Carl Fennessy said he and his brother had always kept an eye on the UK version of MasterChef and believed the category of food and cooking was building as a silent force with the growing popularity of celebrity chefs such as Jamie Oliver, Nigella Lawson and Gordon Ramsay. "It had quietly become sexy to be a chef; we started to use this term 'chefs are the new rock stars'," he said.

"It's been one of the most successful and perennial TV genres of all time, but it had never really been eventised. We tapped into an extraordinary love of food Australians have. There's an expectation now, for a lot of Aussies, you want to be able to cook good bistro quality food in your home."

The Fennessy brothers, running Fremantle Media at the time, licensed the rights to the MasterChef format from Shine. In 2012, the show was taken back to Shine where the brothers now work.

"We always hoped and believed it would be successful, but it was probably more successful that we could have ever anticipated," Mr Fennessy said.

The last decade has seen an unprecedented amount of change in Australian television, in particular Ten has gone through a tumultuous period with highs and lows, including going into administration last year before being bought by US studio giant CBS, but a constant pillar of its programming schedule has been MasterChef.

"There's no doubt, from my perspective, it's not the blockbuster it used to be, but it definitely remains a reliable steady performer within the network," PHD Australia chief executive Mark Coad said. "I think one of the secrets to its enduring success is its focus on the actual craft. I say that, because I think the flavour of a lot of reality TV shows has been a bit salacious, I think MasterChef remains a breath of fresh air."

The show did spawn some successful spin-offs, but following the 4th season of the original not living up to expectations, Ten made a decision to focus purely on the single program.

Mr Fennessy said the secret to MasterChef's success is the show understands what it is and what it stands for.

"It hasn't tried to play the short game, MasterChef has always played the long game and stood by the brand values it stands for," he said.

Supermarket giant Coles will also mark its 10th season with MasterChef and Ten has signed on a record number of sponsors for the show which begins in a week, including; Harvey Norman, Cadbury, Holden, Cobram Estate, Diageo, a2 Milk, Bulla, Pernod Richard, Swisse, Canstar, Ardmona and SATC.

Ten chief executive Paul Anderson said MasterChef was a show that ticked all the boxes from both a commercial and viewer perspective.

HEADLINE: Regional TV urges more deregulation
TEXT:
Regional television broadcasters are urging the Turnbull government to further deregulate the media sector, which would allow them to merge, or risk market failure.

Prime Media, WIN Corp and Southern Cross Austereo were at the forefront of convincing the government to remove the "reach rule", which prevents a TV network from broadcasting to more than 75 per cent of the population, and the "two out of three rule", preventing one entity from owning a TV station, radio network and newspaper in the same market.

The trio warned politicians in their long campaign to change the outdated legislation that more would be required and are now set to push the government to move on the remaining regulation, focusing on the one TV licence to a market rule and two radio licences to a market rule.

"Government requires us to broadcast the same content to regional audiences as their metropolitan cousins watch in the capital cities," Prime chief executive Ian Audsley said. "We are tethered to a metropolitan broadcaster for our content and the cost of content is accelerating at the same time as audiences and advertisers are splintering. Our cost base is tight, with little if any room for further efficiency."

Mr Audsley said consolidation of regional television licences under one operator is the future of regional TV. "Parliamentarians and regulators must understand that the alternative is market failure," he said.

The removal of the one licence to a market for TV would allow regional broadcasters to merge into one business. Bruce Gordon, owner of WIN, is already Prime's largest shareholder with 14.9 per cent.

The initial rules removed last year were to allow the industry to consider potential mergers and acquisitions, although none have come to fruition, as it faces increasing pressure for audience and advertising dollars from digital players such as Google, Facebook, Netflix and Stan, which is 50-50 owned by Nine Entertainment and Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review.

Regional TV broadcasters also face pressure from their metropolitan affiliate partners who have streaming services that broadcast their channels 24/7 and catch up content on-demand via the internet, which faces no legislative restrictions on where it can be sent and is theoretically available to 100 per cent of Australians.

Southern Cross chief executive Grant Blackley said his company supports the abolition of the remaining media ownership restrictions.

"Importantly the one TV licence to a market rule, two radio licences to a market rule and the voices test," he said.

"Removal of these 'traditional media' only rules would be a sensible next step in media reform, particularly in regional markets where it is becoming increasingly difficult for multiple broadcasters to provide a satisfactory level of local content due to the smaller population they serve."

Precedents already exist in smaller regional TV markets. WIN and Prime jointly own a TV licence in remote Western Australia and Mildura where they broadcast Nine content - their affiliate partners are Ten and Seven respectively - and there are licences held by WIN in Mt Gambier, Riverland and Griffith, as well as by Southern Cross in Broken Hill and Spencer Gulf where each broadcast content from all three metro networks.

A spokesman for Communications Minister Mitch Fifield said: "The government has no plans to further amend media ownership and control laws."

Key pointsConsolidation of regional television licences under one operator is the future.

Bruce Gordon, owner of WIN, is Prime's largest shareholder with 14.9 per cent.

HEADLINE: Risks and rewards: the tricky business of sports sponsorship
TEXT:
The perils of sports sponsorship has been a very topical subject of late.

The Australian cricket team ball tampering scandal has rightly focused heavily on the players and the consequences of their actions. But the fallout has gone wider, also placing a lot of attention on the brands and sponsors directly linked to the protagonists, the team and the game of cricket. As a marketer, it raises the pretty big marketing question: are sponsorships still a viable way to market your brand?

Sports sponsorship is a huge global industry, worth more than $65 billion a year today and growing strongly. Why such a big industry? Because, as a marketing tool, when brands get it right, it can be extremely powerful.

A great sponsorship can cut through the sea of sameness in marketing and advertising and really connect and engage the desired audience. In my own career, I've worked for a number of organisations that have been significant sponsors of sport, notably Fosters, Telstra and Visa.

Visa's long-standing sponsorship of the Olympics would be the one I still hold in highest regard. The sponsorship had very clear objectives from the outset: to differentiate Visa from its great rival Mastercard (when there were no notable differences between the two). And, in so doing, to drive worldwide card preference and the perception that Visa was the most accepted card. Visa exceeded expectations and its logo and brand is now synonymous with the Games.

Do all brands get it right? Absolutely not. In my opinion it would be a 50/50 split. And I'm probably being generous. Done badly, sponsorship can end up an expensive waste of time and money.

Why do so many brands stuff it up so badly? They don't get the basics right. It comes down to addressing three key questions. Firstly, what is the brand problem and strategic business objectives that a sponsorship will assist in achieving? Secondly, does the sport/athlete have values that align closely to your own? Thirdly, and critically, how is the sponsorship being brought to life, to achieve your positioning and deliver your commercial objectives?

Sponsorships must be integrated into the entire marketing mix otherwise they are doomed to fail. Branded jerseys, prominent ground signage and a few "proudly supporting" messages just won't cut it. Cosmetic measures such as these don't create meaning for the audience and certainly won't succeed in ultimately getting them to choose your brand over your competitors. Any sponsorship program must be credible and authentic. If it feels forced, it's unlikely to resonate with the very consumers you are trying to reach. In fact, it will likely have the opposite effect and undermine your brand equity.

There also needs to be consideration for what can go wrong. The ball tampering incident isn't the first example of cheating or poor sportsmanship in cricket. Nor will it be the last. The question is how are you going to respond as a sponsor? This needs to be carefully considered before entering any sponsorship agreement. What are your values? Where do you draw the line? Do you claim to stick by your customers in good times and bad but then quickly abandon a sponsorship if an athlete errs, cheats or lies?

Remember also that you enter a sponsorship to connect with fans. This is critical when things do go wrong. My view is Magellan acted far too quickly and pulled its sponsorship of Cricket Australia based on a short-term media frenzy. While cheating is inconsistent with its brand values, which would be the case for all brands, it needed to take a longer-term view. Qantas, which is more experienced in sponsorships and issues management, did the right thing. It waited and was far more considered. It put the fans first.

It's a tricky business when you entrust your brand to other entities, particularly sport. A lot can go wrong. But a lot can go right: you can create something engaging and memorable, and leave a lasting and positive impact on your target customers and, therefore, on the bottom line.

Lisa Ronson is Tourism Australia chief marketing officer.

HEADLINE: Fake news can make old media great again
TEXT:
Fake news can help make old media great again. Amid the growing crisis of trust, it can at least help provide a viable business model for credible, newsroom-based journalism that some fear is dying.

Surprisingly strong gains in paid subscriptions for traditional news mastheads - including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, The Economist and the Financial Times - suggest that digital disruption of the media marketplace has entered a new less-dire phase for journalism. Rewind to peak disruption of half a decade or so ago, when conventional wisdom insisted there was "no such thing as brand". Information demanded to be free. No one would pay for commoditised news that could be easily copied. So it could not pay for the newsrooms that reported it. Even homepages would die, as readers searched in the ether rather than rely on favoured "destination" news sites.

Yet I've just returned from London, getting inside the Financial Times newsroom and business model which has driven print and digital paid audience from 740,000 in 2015 to nearly 930,000 today. That's consistent with The Australian Financial Review's 40 per cent increase in digital retail subscriptions over the same period. For the FT, two-thirds of revenue now comes from content, as opposed to advertising, says chief executive John Ridding. Digital subscribers now make up 80 per cent of the FT's paid audience. Yet the print circulation decline has slowed and the pink FT newspaper remains in the black.

When I last visited the FT, in October 2016, editor Lionel Barber and the newsroom were in a state of shock over the Brexit vote, which they didn't pick. But Brexit and the even bigger populist shock of Donald Trump's presidential win a month later have since generated a surge in paid subscriptions. Brexit and Trump are simply massive stories for an FT-style readership. And, as Ridding says, they also have accelerated the rush to trust amid a mistrusted media ecosystem'.

Social media has polarised politics and media as self-centred readers seek to validate their own world views. But Ridding says that shortchanges business readers who need impartial information on which to base their decisions. Many traditional mastheads responded to digital disruption by trying to quickly build scale on the back of the big social media platforms on which to run an advertising-based business model, Ridding says. Instead, they found that the big platforms sucked away the advertising dollars. So the FT seeks to recreate the habit of print by deeply engaging its digital readers through the integrity of its journalism. "We have to remain true to mission," says Ridding.

The editorial newsroom itself is helping drive this business model, such as through better engaging female readers or building a deals-based franchise similar to the Financial Review's Street Talk. But it also includes big news scoops that boost subscriptions - such as the FT's expose of the sexist London Presidents Club.

At the same time, the scandal of fake news in the US presidential election, and now Facebook's role in it, is returning a trust premium to journalism. This shows up in the Edelman Trust Barometer's finding that Australians' trust in traditional and online-only journalism increased from last year's 41 index points to 52 this year. Trust in search engines and social media platforms as a source of news has fallen from 43 to 38.

Readers are becoming more willing to pay for credible news, just as they now pay for Netflix and Spotify. And the FT is encouraged by the popularity of its digital newsletters. Like a cut-down newspaper, these curated newsletters - such as the Financial Review's Before the Bell and Market Wrap 5pm - help busy readers find the most important news of the day.

Yes, much news has been commoditised. In a world when everyone can be a publisher, media business models were bound to be shaken up. The new models will still include advertising, as in Fairfax Media's world-leading advertising deal with Google. But it could be healthy for journalism to be financed more by the value of what its creates.

Michael Stutchbury is editor in chief of The Australian Financial Review.

HEADLINE: How Fetch built a pay TV challenger to Foxtel
TEXT:
More than a decade ago, Simon Cathcart returned to Australia from Malaysia with an idea, and not much else, to build a subscription television challenger to the dominant market incumbent Foxtel.

Since incorporating the business in April 2008, and launching in 2010, Fetch, run by former Optus executive and ACP magazines boss Scott Lorson, has cemented its place as a credible competitor to Foxtel, having pushed into profitability in December, holding more than 650,000 subscribers and more than $150 million in revenues.

It's been a long road for a business started above a Subway sandwich shop on Sydney's Oxford's Street with no money, no product and no customers.

Mr Cathcart believed the evolution of Australia's broadband market and the lack of alliances between pay TV and telecommunications providers, outside Telstra and Foxtel, meant there was an opening for an internet-delivered subscription TV business. He brought in former colleague Gary Walker to take advantage of the opportunity.

The pair paid for their first flights to business meetings using frequent flyer miles and slowly assembled a small team who thought they were on to something.

"What characterised the first wave of employees was what they had was a tiny team with smaller salaries but big titles," Fetch chief executive Scott Lorson, who joined in 2009, told The Australian Financial Review. "We had more directors than at the Academy Awards because that was required to recruit people on the business."

Mr Cathcart had spent more than a decade in Malaysia working for Astro Malaysia Holdings, one of south-east Asia's biggest media and telco players. Astro Overseas Limited had been loosely involved with Fetch, but in years two and three, it decided to invest big, initially taking a 45 per cent stake in the business, which has now increased to 80 per cent.

"They became more directly involved in the second and third years, seconding staff and eventually providing the significant initial capital to get the idea going," Mr Lorson said.

"However, companies of the calibre of Optus and iiNet are not going to sign long-term exclusive contracts based on a PowerPoint presentation. You actually have to build a product with content, so we literally placed a $30 million bet that if we built the product, we could secure the distribution and the content, and there was this natural opportunity for a legitimate No.2."

Mr Lorson joined in September 2009 and brought in a senior management team, all of whom remain at the business, and they made the radical decision to build their own product in-house, rather than relying on third-party providers. A risk, but one that has ended well for Fetch - it won digital platform of the year at the Australian Home Entertainment Distributors Association awards this month.

"Our shareholder was patient, our partners were patient and we had the talent in the team that were able to find a way through and develop what we now consider to be a best-in-class proposition," Mr Lorson said.

Over the first four years after launching Fetch, brand awareness was near zero, the company did next to no marketing and had only 134,000 subscribers, inching forward at 3000 a month.

The national broadband network and the introduction of bundling with telco partners, which makes up about 80 per cent of sales, which now include Optus, iiNet, Dodo and iPrimus, was a pivotal moment for Fetch. Mr Lorson added the entry of streaming players such as Netflix and Stan, which is 50-50 owned by Nine Entertainment and Fairfax Media, the apps of which are on Fetch boxes, has helped the company push a strategy of "all your entertainment options in one".

The company launched its first major marketing campaign just 12 months ago, co-ordinating with its telco partners. Fetch now has more than 650,000 subscribers and is adding about 12,000 a month.

HEADLINE: Slick Westpac ad runs against the royal commission narrative
TEXT:
For suggesting that the earth might orbit the sun - when it was blindingly obvious to everybody else that the sun orbits the earth - Galileo was convicted of heresy and thrown in jail.

These days we rarely incarcerate contrarians but refusing to toe the popular line can still cause outrage. Which brings me to the latest corporate advertisement from Westpac. The one which depicts people of varying gender, life-stage and ethnic extraction being rescued from daunting situations by their workmates, peers and neighbours to the accompaniment of a cover of the David Bowie classic Heroes.

At a minute-and-a-half it's an extremely long ad, and I must confess that for the first nail-biting, heart-rending, no-expense-spared 85 seconds I wondered if it might actually be a trailer for a new Australian movie - the next Baz Luhrmann extravaganza, perhaps. But just when I expected to hear a gravelly voice saying "Coming soon to a cinema near you" up popped the end frame with a big fat Westpac logo, and alongside it a strapline which makes everything clear: Help when it matters. It's what Australians do.

Of course it is. Bloody oath. Well said. Are we not, after all, the nation that invented mateship? Are we not the home of the fair go? Are we not … But hang on a moment. Are we not also the country whose big banks are the subject of a royal commission? And is that royal commission not the consequence of decades of complaints from customers and consumer watchdogs and the mainstream media that they care more about shareholders than customers?

Indeed, are the big banks not so on the nose with the public right now that to atone for both acknowledged sins and whatever additional misdemeanours the royal commission might expose, their spokesbody, the Australian Bankers Association, has been campaigning on their collective behalf. One of the components of that campaign is a TV ad which rationalises bank profitability by pointing out that while its principal beneficiaries are indeed shareholders, most of those shareholders are, pace their super funds, ordinary Australians.

Whether or not you are persuaded by this argument, one thing that impressed me about this ABA TV ad is how, well, unimpressive it is. The locations are real bank offices, the "talent" are real bank staff, and nothing has been done in the way of make-up, wardrobe, lighting and editing to make them or the job they do look in the least bit interesting or glamorous; it's like a Bunnings ad without the specials. As such it will probably not win any creative awards. But if the brief is to convince people that Australian banks don't waste the money that you entrust to them, a conspicuously no-frills ad campaign will certainly help. As will demonstrating that while some bank employees might be, like many ordinary Australians, a bit overweight, most of them are by no means fat cats, and that they take a modest pride in providing what they see as a public service.

I have no idea what Westpac spent making its ad, but given the huge cast, multiple locations and sophisticated post-production effects - not to mention the use of a famous David Bowie song - I'd be surprised if it was south of $3 million. And there is nothing modest about an organisation that allies itself with acts of heroism. But perhaps the ABA, and the government, and the media, and all the other banks have all got it all wrong. Perhaps Westpac is the Galileo of Australian finance.

Simon Collins is co-founder and creative consultant at Collins Gartrell.
